blocks.h: Why a trie instead of a set of words?
p: A set answers `search` in O(L) hashing but can't answer `startsWith` without scanning every word. The trie shares prefixes, so a prefix query is a single walk of length equal to the prefix. The `'$'` key assumes real letters never equal `'$'`, which holds for lowercase words.

bullets: Time: O(L) per operation, where L is the length of the word or prefix.
Space: O(total characters inserted) in the worst case (less when words share prefixes).

208.takeaway: A trie stores words as paths of characters with an end-of-word flag; prefix and exact search are the same walk with different final checks.

blocks.h: Why is `.` handled by DFS and the rest by a plain walk?
p: A letter has exactly one place to go, so the search stays a single path (like a normal trie). A `.` fans out into every child, so the search branches. Each `.` can multiply the work by up to 26, which is where the O(26^k) worst case comes from (k dots).
`'$'` is stored in the same dict as letters. Without `if k != '$'`, a `.` could 'match' the marker key and recurse into `True` (a bool, not a dict), causing an error or false matches.

bullets: Time: addWord: O(L). search: O(L) with no dots; worst case O(26^k · L) with k dots over a dense trie.
Space: O(total characters stored), plus O(L) recursion depth.

211.takeaway: Trie plus DFS: plain letters follow one child, a wildcard tries all children.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Inverts both subtrees, then assigns them swapped
Tuple assignment: the right-hand side is fully evaluated first, then the two targets are set
Lets the parent assign the inverted child; the tree is modified in place

blocks.h: Why does the one-liner not need a temp variable?
p: Python evaluates the right side `(invert(right), invert(left))` completely, producing two already-inverted subtrees, before it assigns them. At that point `root.left` and `root.right` still point to the old children, so the assignment can overwrite both safely. The recursive calls first invert each subtree internally, then the parent swaps their places.

blocks.h: Why does the order of recursion not matter?
p: Inverting the left and right subtrees are independent operations (they share no nodes), so either could run first. Only the final swap must happen after both are done, which the tuple assignment guarantees.

bullets: Time: O(n) — each node visited once.
Space: O(h) recursion depth (O(n) for a degenerate chain).

226.takeaway: Invert a tree by recursively inverting both children and swapping them.

p: Operations `push(1), push(2), peek(), pop(), push(3), pop(), pop()`. The right end of each list is the top of that stack:

blocks.h: Why transfer only when `out` is empty?
p: If you moved items while `out` still held some, the new items would end up on top of older ones and come out first, which would break FIFO order. Here `3` waits in `inp` while `2` is still in `out`, so `2` comes out before `3`.

Each item is pushed on `inp` once, moved to `out` once and popped once, i.e. a constant number of operations per item over its lifetime. A single `pop` can cost O(n) if it triggers a big transfer, but then the next n−1 operations are O(1).

bullets: Time: push O(1); pop/peek O(1) amortised (O(n) worst case for one call).
Space: O(n) for the items stored.

232.takeaway: Queue from two stacks: push onto an input stack, pop from an output stack, and refill it by reversing only when it's empty.

blocks.h: Why does the first split node have to be the answer?
p: Every common ancestor lies on the path from the root, and all nodes above the split point send both targets the same way, so they are common ancestors but not the lowest. The first node where `p` and `q` go to different children (or where one of them is the node itself) has both in its subtree, and no lower node does. That is also why a node counts as its own ancestor: for `p=2, q=4` we stop at 2 itself.

p: Words `['practice', 'makes', 'perfect', 'coding', 'makes']`. Positions: {'practice': [0], 'makes': [1, 4], 'perfect': [2], 'coding': [3]}. Query `shortest('makes', 'coding')` with a = [1, 4], b = [3]:

blocks.h: Why advance the pointer at the smaller position?
p: With a[i] < b[j], pairing a[i] with any later b (larger than b[j]) only increases the distance, so a[i] is finished. Moving `i` is the only move that can find a closer pair. Each step retires one position, so the loop is O(a + b). `shortest('coding','practice')` is just 3 from a single comparison of [3] with [0].
When many queries are made on the same list, paying O(n) once is cheaper. Queries only touch the positions of the two words involved.

bullets: Time: Constructor O(n); each query O(a + b), where a and b are the occurrence counts of the two words.
Space: O(n) for all position lists.

244.takeaway: Precompute word → sorted positions, then merge two sorted position lists with two pointers, always advancing the smaller.

blocks.h: Why a heap and not a sorted list or a counter?
p: We need the minimum end time repeatedly while inserting new ones, which is exactly a priority queue's job.

Reusing a room means replacing its old end time by the new one. `heapq.heapreplace(heap, end)` does that in one call, but the pop/push pair is equivalent and the heap size (rooms) only grows when no room was free.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) — sorting plus n heap operations of O(log n).
Space: O(n) in the worst case, when all meetings overlap.

253.takeaway: Sort by start and keep a min-heap of end times: reuse the earliest-free room if it's free, otherwise open a new one; the heap size is the answer.

head: Code

When to reach for it
rows: Cheapest and second-cheapest totals for the previous house, and the colour that gave `min1`
Enough to answer 'cheapest total with a different colour' for any colour
If this colour equals the previous best colour use the runner-up, otherwise the best
Enforces the neighbour constraint without scanning k colours
`if total < n1: n1, n2, n_idx = total, n1, j` / `elif total < n2`
Maintain the two smallest totals and the colour of the smallest
One pass tracks top-2 without sorting

p: `[[1,5,3],[2,9,4]]`. Each cell is cost + previous min (min2 only for the colour that gave min1). Answer: 5.

For colour j the best previous total is the smallest over all colours except j. If j is not the colour that gave the overall minimum, that minimum itself works (`min1`). If it is, the best remaining one is the second minimum (`min2`). So two numbers answer all k questions, turning the naive O(n·k²) into O(n·k).

`elif total < n2` only runs when `total` didn't beat `n1`; when it does beat `n1`, the old `n1` is demoted to `n2` in the same statement. Ties in totals are fine: either colour can serve as `idx`, and the runner-up value then equals the best, so nothing is lost.

bullets: Time: O(n·k).
Space: O(1) beyond the input.

265.takeaway: k-colour DP with top-2 tracking: the best previous cost for colour j is min1 unless j produced min1, then min2.

p: Across the whole run, `x` XORs every number in `0..n` (the indices `0..n-1` plus `n`) and every array value. Each number present in the array appears twice and cancels, so what is left is the one number in `0..n` that appears only once (as an index/`n`): the missing value, 2.
